The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the national rollout of the cashless debit card, but supported extending existing trials in Ceduna, East Kimberley, and Goldfields until June 2020 to avoid disruption. Labor will move an amendment allowing people to leave the card if they demonstrate responsible financial management, and criticised the government for relying on the flawed ORIMA evaluation.

The bill would let the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation finance more overseas infrastructure projects that benefit Australia.
It would give Efic a new power to back projects based on an Australian benefit test and raise its callable capital by $1 billion.
Efic could also operate under the trading name Export Finance Australia.
Increases Efic's callable capital by $1 billion.
Grants Efic a new overseas infrastructure financing power.
Allows Efic to use the trading name Export Finance Australia.
The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation and Australian businesses involved in regional infrastructure projects.

The majority voted in favour of the main idea of the bill, which means the Senate can now discuss it in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What does the bill do? The bill [was introduced to](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6263): > *expand the ability of the [Export Finance and Insurance Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_Finance_and_Insurance_Corporation) to finance infrastructure projects by increasing its [callable capital](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/callable-capital) and granting it a new overseas infrastructure financing power.*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2019-04-03.217.1) to pass the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6263) in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). The bill was introduced to: > *expand the ability of the [Export Finance and Insurance Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_Finance_and_Insurance_Corporation) to finance infrastructure projects by increasing its callable capital and granting it a new overseas infrastructure financing power.*

The opposition supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which provides Efic with an extra $1 billion in callable capital, renames it Export Finance Australia, and introduces an Australian benefits test for loans funding Pacific infrastructure; the bill was referred to a Senate inquiry reporting by 26 March 2019. The speech noted bipartisan backing, citing Bill Shorten's proposed Pacific infrastructure investment bank and the government's $2 billion Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific, and suggested examining the US BUILD Act and UK CDC Group as alternative models.

The bill provides the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation with an additional $1 billion in capital for commercial infrastructure loans in the Pacific, subject to an Australian benefit test. The speaker also criticised the coalition government for neglecting Pacific relations, particularly through climate change inaction and $11 billion in aid cuts.

The speaker argued that Australia should support Pacific infrastructure through the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill 2019, providing an additional $1 billion in callable capital for loans on a commercial basis, to boost regional prosperity, security, and economic integration while also benefiting Australian exporters like those in Tasmania.

The speaker argued that the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill is welcome but overdue, and criticised the government for failing to take the Pacific seriously, citing the Prime Minister's absence from the September Pacific Islands Forum, Environment Minister Melissa Price's reported "chequebook" comment to former Kiribati president Anote Tong, and the agriculture visa debacle, while supporting the Seasonal Worker Program and calling for a credible climate change policy.

The speaker supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which renames Efic to Export Finance Australia and provides an extra $1 billion in callable capital for infrastructure financing in the Pacific, including East Timor, with a new Australian benefits test replacing the previous one-third Australian content requirement. The speaker noted bipartisan agreement on Pacific funding, referenced the opposition leader’s October 2018 announcement and the Prime Minister’s subsequent similar announcement, and called for Senate committee scrutiny to address concerns about project quality and unintended consequences.

The speaker expressed concerns about the bill's $1 billion increase in callable capital for Efic and the lack of accompanying policy frameworks, noted Labor's prior proposal for a government-backed infrastructure investment bank, and criticised the government for cutting $11 billion in development assistance over five years.

The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019 received bipartisan support to enhance Australia's infrastructure investment in the Pacific, with Efic to operate under the trading name Export Finance Australia.

The Greens moved an amendment to prohibit the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation (Efic) from funding or facilitating thermal coal mining and export on a commercial scale, including projects like the Adani coalmine, and criticised the government for secretly altering Efic's mandate in 2017 to allow coal funding.
Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Act 2019
The bill would let the Secretary of the Department of Health appoint a wider range of people as authorised officers to enforce the Tobacco Plain Packaging Act.

Currently only federal public servants and Australian Federal Police members can be appointed; the bill would add people employed by other Commonwealth entities, state or territory health or police officers, and local government officials with health or tobacco enforcement duties.

The change is designed to handle future organisational changes, such as the National Measurement Institute restructuring, and to allow local officers to respond to non-compliance in remote areas, but only with the agreement of the relevant state or territory.
Expands the categories of persons eligible to be appointed as authorised officers under the Act.
Allows state and territory police officers and local government officials to be appointed with the consent of their jurisdiction.
Responds to potential future organisational changes, such as the National Measurement Institute altering its employment arrangements.

The Department of Health, the National Measurement Institute, state and territory health departments, state and territory police, and local government officials with health or tobacco enforcement responsibilities.

The majority voted in favour of [government amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-11.4.2) (1) to (5) and (8) to (11), which means they succeeded. ### What do these amendments do? These amendments would move several matters that are currently in disallowable instruments - that is, legislative instruments that the parliament is able to vote against in a single vote so they stop being law - to standard legislation that can't so easily be undone. These matters include the location of the trial sites. According to Liberal MP [Mitch Fifield](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/mitch_fifield), who introduced the amendments, *"[this will give certainty](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-09-11.6.1) to trial participants and local communities"*. ### What does the bill do? The [bill was introduced to](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6130): * *expand the cashless debit card arrangements to a further trial site, the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay area, to run until 30 June 2020;* * *specify the class of trial participants for the area and increase the total number of trial participants overall to 15 000;* * *provide for an exception from the restrictive trade practices provisions of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 for merchants that implement product level blocking systems to identify that a cashless debit card is being used for payment and, if any restricted products are being purchased, decline the transaction; and* * *limit the use of the restricted portion of a payment to prevent the portion being used to obtain cash-like products which could be used to obtain alcohol or gambling.*

The bill expands the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, covering around 6,700 people under 36 on Newstart, youth allowance, or parenting payments, running until 30 June 2020, based on community consultation and evidence of intergenerational welfare dependency.

The speaker argued against expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing a woeful evaluation, no reduction in violence, and a damning Auditor-General's report, while supporting continuation of existing trials in Ceduna and East Kimberley for two years. The bill would give the Federal Circuit Court of Australia the power to issue injunctions or order compensation when a supplier breaks the Commonwealth Procurement Rules for a covered procurement.

A supplier would have to lodge a complaint with the relevant Commonwealth entity's accountable authority and have it investigated, and the procurement would be paused unless a public interest certificate is in force, before going to court.

The bill aims to help Australia meet its international trade obligations, such as those under the World Trade Organization Agreement on Government Procurement and the Trans-Pacific Partnership Agreement, and to give regional and small businesses easier access to justice.
Vests the Federal Circuit Court with jurisdiction to grant injunctions and order compensation for procurement rule breaches.
Requires suppliers to complain to the accountable authority first and have the procurement suspended during investigation, unless a public interest certificate applies.
Enables Australia to meet international obligations on government procurement complaints and remedies.
Suppliers, including regional and small and medium enterprises, and Commonwealth entities involved in covered procurements.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-10-18.83.1) to pass the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5871). In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1819a/19bd026): > *The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 (the Bill) proposes to fill a gap in the current arrangements in administrative law relating to Commonwealth procurement, and to address obligations under relevant free trade agreements, by creating new rules for making and investigating complaints in relation to the contravention of relevant Commonwealth Procurement Rules (CPRs).*

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill establishes an independent complaints mechanism for Commonwealth procurement, designating the Federal Circuit Court to review breaches of the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, with compensation limited to reasonable tender preparation costs, and requiring suppliers to first complain to the procuring entity.

Labor supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 to give small and medium businesses cheaper, faster court access for procurement disputes, but moved an amendment criticising the government for not maximising opportunities in the $50 billion annual procurement program.

The speaker supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 and an amendment, but criticised procurement policies for overlooking local economic benefits, citing the defence dress uniforms contract from Bendigo's Australian Defence Apparel being sent to Vietnam, costing 50–70 local jobs, and argued for greater local content and WTO standards to counter illegal dumping.

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 expands the Federal Circuit Court's jurisdiction to hear disputes under the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, allowing it to grant injunctions and order compensation for breaches. The speaker also argued that Commonwealth procurement should prioritise local Australian suppliers, particularly small and medium enterprises, and consider broader economic benefits like tax receipts and multiplier effects, not just immediate value for money.

The speaker supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 with an amendment but criticised its timing, arguing it should wait until WTO Government Procurement Agreement accession is resolved, and noted that past trade agreements like the Australia-US Free Trade Agreement underdelivered on Australian access to foreign contracts. The speech also highlighted $47–60 billion in annual Commonwealth procurement, risks to small and medium enterprises, and called for using procurement to achieve broader goals such as human rights compliance, environmental sustainability, and stronger Australian industry participation, citing weak requirements in the Future Submarine program.

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 adds an appeals mechanism to the Commonwealth Procurement Rules to comply with free trade agreements, but the speaker emphasised that Australian small and medium businesses face major barriers to winning government contracts, with Defence accounting for $112 billion of the $217 billion in procurement from 2012–13 to 2016–17, and the 10% SME target undermined by competition from international firms and costly panel arrangements.

The speaker argued that the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017, implementing Trans-Pacific Partnership and WTO Government Procurement Agreement commitments, weakens Australia's ability to favour local businesses by making it easier for foreign entities to challenge government contracts. The speaker noted that in 2015–16, Commonwealth agencies entered 70,338 contracts worth $56.9 billion, with total government procurement estimated at $120 billion annually, and criticised the government for not broadening 'value for money' to include whole-of-life benefits.

The member moved an amendment to defer the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 until the Trans-Pacific Partnership and WTO Agreement on Government Procurement include better protections for labour, the environment and local business and remove investor-state dispute settlement provisions. The bill was opposed on the grounds that it would let multinational corporations sue the Australian government, disadvantage local businesses, and was being rushed through without the final trade agreement text being seen.

The speaker argued that free trade policies have destroyed Australian manufacturing and agriculture, citing closures of the motor vehicle, whitegoods, textile, steel, cement, sugar, dairy and wool industries, with specific declines of 23% in beef, 31% in dairy and 72% in sheep numbers. He called for restoring sovereignty by requiring all government-procured motor vehicles to be Australian-made.

The speaker argued that the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 creates an independent complaints mechanism for procurement, giving regional and small suppliers timely access to justice, and noted that 95% of contracts (worth $40.8 billion) were awarded to Australian suppliers in 2016–17.

The majority voted in favour of [reporting the bill](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). In light of the [previous vote](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/senate/2018-08-22/2), the bill is in an unusual situation meaning that after this vote it will effectively fail. An [interaction](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-08-22.16.3) between South Australian Senator [Penny Wong](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/penny_wong) (Labor) and the Chair explains. Senator Wong: > *The Senate has just voted against a motion that the bill stand as printed. Given that was somewhat unusual, although I think it has occurred before, it might be useful for the chair to advise the Senate what the status of the next vote signifies so senators can be clear what they're voting on and whether there will, in fact, be a third reading.* The Chair: > *Thank you, Senator Wong.
